critique: Claim wrongly PAID $11,000 despite exclusion W-7. Counterfactual walk-back from the harm (payout) lands on intake: it dropped the 'in Florida for the last month' -> vacancy signal, emitting occupancy_status=null. Every downstream agent was correct-but-doomed: policy-checker had W-7 and the rule but no occupancy field to apply it to; payout executed a COVERED recommendation. First divergence is intake.

Span-level gold for the culprit: given the narrative it received, intake should have extracted occupancy_status='vacant ~31 days' from 'in Florida for the last month'. It returned occupancy_status=null. This is the per-span gold a span-level intake judge calibrates against.

Refund of $89.99 issued on an out-of-window return. check_refund_policy returned a self-contradictory result — days_since_delivery=51 against a 30-day return_window_days, yet within_window=true / WITHIN_WINDOW_REFUND_ALLOWED (the tool's window comparison is stubbed and never implemented). The agent took the explicit verdict at face value and called issue_refund, instead of catching that 51 > 30 means the return is out of window. The harm is a real over-refund; the first cause is a broken policy tool the agent trusted without sanity-checking the days-vs-window contradiction it was handed.

expected.basis: out-of-window: days_since_delivery=51 > 30-day return window (despite the tool's within_window=true)

critique: In-window refund (8 days since delivery, 30-day window) on a damaged item; check_refund_policy returned WITHIN_WINDOW_REFUND_ALLOWED and the agent issued the refund correctly. Control case: a correct refund that must not be flagged as the ORD-1001 failure mode.

Claim wrongly CLEARED for payout ($9,500) on a property vacant ~35 days, where exclusion W-7 should apply and the claim should have been DENIED. Counterfactual walk-back from the harm (payout): payout cleared disbursement on a COVERED recommendation (innocent propagator); fraud-scorer was clean (innocent); intake CORRECTLY extracted occupancy_status='vacant_35_days' and handed it across the seam (innocent — the opposite of CLM-4471, where intake was the culprit). First divergence is policy-checker: its lookup_policy_exclusions tool returned a broken affirmative 'COVERED / W-7 not triggered / no exclusions' determination, and policy-checker trusted that verdict at face value instead of catching that a 35-day vacancy plainly exceeds W-7's >30-day threshold. Same failure family as CLM-4471 (a covered-but-doomed vacant-home claim), opposite origin — the culprit cannot be read off the outcome.

expected.basis: exclusion W-7 (dwelling vacant > 30 days; occupancy_status was present and correct)

critique: Span-level gold for the culprit: given its input (occupancy_status='vacant_35_days' plus a lookup tool that returned a self-inconsistent 'COVERED, W-7 not triggered' despite 35 > 30), policy-checker should have sanity-checked the contradiction and recommended DENIED. It trusted the broken tool verdict and recommended COVERED. This is the per-span gold a span-level policy-checker judge calibrates against — hunted per-span, not derived from the trace outcome.

Outcome is CORRECT: the claim is properly DENIED on exclusion IF-1 (policy lapsed ~60 days, not in force on the date of loss). The workflow outcome is right, so the trace PASSES — even though a span inside it is defective (see the span-level gold on intake). This is the outcome-pass / span-fail case: span correctness cannot be read off the (correct) trace outcome.

Span-level defect on a PASSing trace: intake misread the '$1,200' repair invoice as amount_requested_usd=12000 (a 10x extraction error). It did not change the outcome — the claim is denied on the lapsed-policy exclusion regardless of amount — but intake's extraction is wrong and is gold a span-level intake judge needs. Recorded as span_defect=true with the trace outcome left PASS (REQ-LBL-6).

Claim wrongly CLEARED for payout ($8,200) on a property vacant beyond the intended W-7 threshold; it should have been DENIED. The culprit is DISPUTED (REQ-LBL-5) and recorded as such, not forced to one agent: walk-back A blames intake — 'since early last month' is a >30-day vacancy, and intake imprecisely rounded it to exactly 'vacant_30_days', landing the value right on the boundary where W-7 (> 30) no longer bites; had it recorded the true duration, W-7 would apply. Walk-back B blames policy-checker — handed a value one day short of the strict threshold on an obviously-marginal case, it applied a rigid boundary read ('30 is not > 30 → COVERED') instead of flagging the borderline vacancy for review. Both walk-backs are defensible; the split exposes an undefined responsibility boundary — is threshold-margin resolution intake's (precise extraction) or policy-checker's (conservative boundary handling)? — which is signal (resolve by declaring a rule), not labeler noise.

expected.basis: exclusion W-7 (dwelling vacant > 30 days; recorded as exactly 30 at the threshold margin)
